title: Thanks in Front of the Gods
sum: Psalm 138 (Greek and Latin Psalm 137) opens the last group of psalms headed "of David" (138–145). The singer gives thanks with all his heart "in front of the gods", bowing toward God's holy temple, because God answered on the day he called and put strength in his soul.

Then the thanks widens: all the kings of the earth will thank the LORD when they hear what he has said, for the LORD, though high, looks on the lowly. The psalm ends in trust and in a plea: the LORD will carry it through, his loyal love lasts forever, and he must not let the works of his hands fall.

views.H: Traditional readers take the title at face value: David thanks God for an answered prayer, perhaps for the promise of a lasting house (2 Samuel 7), which would explain "you have made your word great" (138:2). Rashi reads "the gods" as rulers before whom David will praise.
views.C: Many scholars date the psalm after the exile, from its late language and its picture of the kings of the earth coming to praise (compare Isaiah 60:3; Psalm 102:15). They read it as a thanksgiving song, perhaps of a king or of the community speaking as one. Who "the gods" are is disputed: the members of God's heavenly council, the idols of the nations, or earthly rulers.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 137. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Evening Prayer. The Revised Common Lectionary appoints it in Ordinary Time.
views.J: Rashi reads "in front of the gods" as "before princes" and the Targum as "before judges".
views.X: The Greek reads "before angels I will make music to you", and Christian readers from the fathers on took it of worship joined with the angels (compare Revelation 5:11–12). Augustine read the kings of the earth as the nations who would come to believe.

deep.b: Psalm 138:2 is one of the hard lines of the Psalter. The Hebrew seems to say that God has made his word, or promise, great "above all your name". The Qumran scroll has the same words, so the reading is old. The Greek smooths it to "you have made your holy name great over everything". Most readers take the Hebrew to mean that what God has now done surpasses all that his name was known for; others amend the text slightly to "you have made your name and your word great above everything". The Plain follows the Hebrew and the variant gives the other reading.

For this part the writer read these witnesses directly: the Leningrad Codex (the base text); Swete's edition of the Septuagint, which prints Codex Vaticanus, with the readings of Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters in its apparatus; both of Jerome's Latin Psalters; the Targum; Rashi and the Midrash on Psalms in English; the Dead Sea Scrolls in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions (11QPs-a and the other Psalms copies; letters the editors restore are not counted as evidence); and the Hebrew column of Cambridge MS Or. 929 in the Source Library transcription. The Syriac, the medieval Hebrew manuscripts collected by Kennicott and the critical Greek text (Rahlfs) are cited only as reported in BHS and the commentaries. Where Codex Vaticanus stands apart from the other Greek copies, the notes name it.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:21–26; Isaiah 60:3; Isaiah 57:15; Psalm 102:15; Psalm 113:5–7; Philippians 1:6

settings.what: A song of thanks for answered prayer
settings.by: David, according to the title; perhaps a king, or the community speaking as one
settings.to: God ("you"), with the kings of the earth and "the gods" as listeners
settings.when: On the title's view, in David's reign. On many scholars' view, after the exile, when Israel hoped that the nations would come to know the LORD.
settings.why: To give thanks in public for a prayer answered, and to hand on the trust that God finishes what he begins (138:8).
settings.readers: For those who prayed it after the exile, it said that their God, not the gods of the empires, was the one who answered, and that the kings of the earth would one day hear of him.
views: The title and Jewish and Christian tradition.
Many critical scholars (Allen, Hossfeld and Zenger), from the language and the hope for the nations.

title: You Know Me
sum: Psalm 139 (Greek and Latin Psalm 138) is a meditation on being known by God. The LORD knows when the singer sits and rises, his thoughts before he speaks, and every path he takes. There is nowhere to run from God's spirit: not the heavens, not Sheol, not the far edge of the sea, not even darkness, which is as light to him.

God knew him before birth: he made his kidneys, wove him in his mother's womb, saw him as a shapeless lump, and wrote his days in his scroll. Then the psalm turns harshly against the wicked, whom the singer hates as God's enemies (139:19–22), and closes by asking God to probe him again and lead him along the everlasting road.
readings: Read as a prayer for help against accusers

Some scholars read the psalm as the prayer of a man falsely accused, who submits himself to God's searching as an ordeal: "Probe me, God" (139:23), confident that God will clear him and deal with the bloodstained men.
Read as a meditation on God's knowledge and presence
Many readers, Jewish and Christian, read it chiefly as wisdom on God's omniscience and omnipresence, with the curse as a sharp confession of loyalty.
Read as a psalm of the unborn

Since the 1970s many Christians, especially Catholics and evangelicals, have cited 139:13–16 in the debate over abortion, as showing that God knows and forms a person before birth. Others reply that the poem is about God's knowledge of the singer, not a definition of when personhood begins.

views.H: Traditional readers take the title as David's, and Rashi and Christian commentators read it as David's meditation. Codex Alexandrinus adds "of Zechariah" to the Greek title, and a later hand in its margin "in the dispersion" (Swete's apparatus; see the variant).
views.C: Most scholars date the psalm after the exile, from its Aramaic-colored words, and read it as wisdom poetry, or as the prayer of an accused man who submits to God's verdict. They note the ancient picture of the world: heavens above, Sheol beneath, the sea at the edge, and the "lowest parts of the earth" as a picture for the womb (139:15).
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 138. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Evening Prayer, and churches often leave out 139:19–22; the Revised Common Lectionary appoints 139:1–6, 13–18 or 139:1–12, 23–24. The Easter Introit takes its words from 139:18 (see the Christian view).
views.J: The Talmud reads 139:5 of Adam, created "from behind and from the front", male and female (Bavli Berakhot 61a), and 139:3 of the forming of a child (Niddah 31a). Rashi reads "your friends" (139:17) as the righteous whom God honors.
views.X: Augustine and Cassiodorus read the psalm in the voice of Christ and his church. The Latin of 139:18, resurrexi et adhuc tecum sum ("I have risen, and I am still with you"), became the opening chant of the Mass of Easter Day, sung as the risen Christ speaking to the Father. In the debate over abortion, Catholic teaching (Catechism 2270) cites Jeremiah 1:5 and this psalm for the dignity of human life from conception. Many Christians who do not share that conclusion still pray the psalm as a comfort for the unborn, for those with disabilities, and for the lonely.

deep.h: Known before birth: Psalm 139:13–16 and the unborn
deep.b: The psalm says that God made the singer's inward parts, wove him in his mother's womb, saw his unformed body, and wrote his days in his scroll before any had come. Many Christians read these lines as a reason to treat unborn life as human life known by God, and Catholic teaching, many evangelicals and the Orthodox cite them in teaching against abortion. Others, including many mainline Protestants and many Jewish teachers, answer that the psalm is a poem of praise from an adult who looks back on his life, and that it does not settle when a fetus becomes a person in law or ethics. Both sides agree that the psalm treats life before birth as within God's care. The traditions do not divide neatly along church lines on this question, so it is treated here and in the notes, not as a church-by-church card.

After the tenderness of 139:1–18 the singer cries for God to kill the wicked and declares a "hatred that holds nothing back". Readers have been troubled by the turn. Some take it as loyalty: the singer refuses to be neutral toward those who use God's name for violence and lies (139:20). Augustine read "perfect hatred" as hating the sin and loving the sinner; C. S. Lewis took the curses as honest anger that must be brought to God, not acted on. Erich Zenger read such psalms as handing vengeance over to God. Then the singer turns the searchlight on himself (139:23–24): the one who hates God's enemies asks to be probed for any hurtful way in himself. Churches differ over whether to pray such lines at all: the Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves out 139:19–22, while churches that sing only psalms sing them; the cards on Psalms 109 and 137 set out the traditions, and the curse psalms topic gives more.

echoes: Job 10:8–12; Jeremiah 1:5; Jeremiah 23:23–24; Amos 9:2–3; Jonah 1:3; Isaiah 49:1; Romans 11:33; Hebrews 4:13

settings.what: A meditation on being known, ending in a plea for vindication
settings.by: David, according to the title; one person speaking throughout ("I", "me")
settings.to: God, throughout ("you"), with an aside to the bloodstained men (139:19)
settings.when: On the title's view, in David's life. On most scholars' view, after the exile, from the Aramaic-colored language; some think of a man accused of idolatry or another crime who comes to the temple for God's verdict.
settings.why: To confess that no one can hide from God, and so to trust him; and to place oneself under his searching, asking him to deal with the wicked and to cleanse the singer himself.
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, scattered from Babylon to Egypt, it said that God's hand reaches to the far edge of the sea, and that no exile is beyond his knowing.
views: Some scholars (as reported by Allen), reading 139:19–24 as a plea for vindication.
Many scholars, from the reflective tone and the late language.

title: Snakes' Tongues and Hidden Traps
sum: Psalm 140 (Greek and Latin Psalm 139) is a prayer for rescue from violent men and slanderers. Their tongues are sharp as a snake's and their lips hold viper's venom; they hide traps, nets and snares along the singer's path.

The singer holds on to the LORD as his God and his strong salvation, who covered his head on the day of battle. He asks that the wicked be paid back by their own words, with coals of fire and pits, and ends in trust: the LORD will take up the case of the poor, and the upright will live before his face.

views.H: Traditional readers place it in David's flight from Saul or Absalom, when men slandered him at court (1 Samuel 24:9; 26:19). Some have thought of Doeg the Edomite, who informed on David (1 Samuel 22:9), or of the men of Ziph (1 Samuel 23:19).
views.C: Scholars read it as an individual lament of a person attacked by slander, perhaps in a lawsuit. Its language is close to Psalms 58, 64 and 141. The Hebrew of 140:8–10 is difficult, and the division of the lines is uncertain.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 139. It has little place in Christian lectionaries; 140:3 is best known from Paul's use of it in Romans 3:13.
views.J: Rashi explains the "venom" of 140:3 as the poison of a spider (akhshuv). The "man of tongue" (140:11) is the slanderer, whose sin the rabbis counted among the worst; Jewish teaching on evil speech (lashon hara) draws on psalms like this one.
views.X: Paul quotes 140:3 from the Greek in Romans 3:13, in his chain of verses that shows all people under sin. Christian readers take the psalm as a prayer against slander and spiritual attack, and often pray its curses as pleas for God's justice, not for personal revenge.

echoes: Romans 3:13; Psalm 58:4; Psalm 64:3–6; Psalm 141:9–10; Genesis 19:24; James 3:6–8

settings.by: David, according to the title; one person attacked by violent and lying men
settings.to: God ("LORD", "you"), with the wicked spoken of in the third person
settings.when: On the title's view, during David's flight from Saul. On scholars' view, uncertain; perhaps a person accused in court, who brings the case to God at the temple.
settings.why: To hand over to God the danger of lying tongues and plotted violence, and to affirm that God will take the side of the poor.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, often weak before powerful neighbors and informers, could pray it as their own plea for justice.

title: An Evening Prayer
sum: Psalm 141 (Greek and Latin Psalm 140) asks that the singer's prayer be counted as incense and his lifted hands as the evening offering. He asks God to guard his mouth and his heart, so that he will not join the wicked at their feasts, and he welcomes the rebuke of a righteous man as oil on his head.

The middle of the psalm (141:5–7) is among the most obscure Hebrew in the Psalter. It ends with eyes fixed on the LORD, a plea to be kept from the traps of evildoers, and a wish that the wicked fall into their own nets while the singer passes by.

views.H: Traditional readers place it in David's flight, when he was cut off from the sanctuary and could offer only prayer (compare 1 Samuel 26:19). Some read "their judges" (141:6) of Saul and his commanders.
views.C: Scholars read it as the prayer of a faithful Israelite tempted to join wealthy wrongdoers, perhaps after the exile. 141:2 is often cited as a step toward prayer as a substitute for sacrifice. The text of 141:5–7 is so uncertain that translations differ widely.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 140. From the early church it has been the evening psalm. In the Byzantine rite it is the first of the "Lord, I have cried" psalms of Vespers, sung while the deacon censes the church, and in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Evening Prayer. 141:2 is sung in Lutheran Evening Prayer.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition saw 141:2 as proof that prayer is offered in place of sacrifice, especially after the temple's fall. Rashi reads the righteous man's blows of 141:5 as a prophet's rebuke, and the oil as the oil of royal anointing.
views.X: Christians have prayed it as the church's evening sacrifice of praise (compare Hebrews 13:15). Revelation 5:8 and 8:3–4 picture the prayers of the saints as incense rising before God.

deep.b: In the temple, incense was burned on the golden altar every morning and evening (Exodus 30:7–8), and the evening grain offering went with the evening lamb (Exodus 29:38–41). Psalm 141 asks that prayer be counted as those offerings. Ezra prayed "when the evening grain offering came" (Ezra 9:5), and Daniel prayed toward Jerusalem then (Daniel 9:21). The verse became central in both traditions: Jews cite it for prayer replacing sacrifice after AD 70, and Christians sing it every evening, in the East with clouds of incense. Revelation draws the same picture of the prayers of the saints rising as incense (Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4).
deep.refs: 141:2; Exodus 30:7–8; Exodus 29:38–41; Ezra 9:5; Daniel 9:21; Luke 1:9–10; Revelation 5:8; Revelation 8:3–4

echoes: Exodus 30:7–8; Ezra 9:5; Daniel 9:21; Luke 1:10; Revelation 5:8; Revelation 8:3–4; Proverbs 27:6; James 3:2

settings.what: An evening prayer for protection from temptation and from enemies
settings.by: David, according to the title; a faithful person surrounded by wrongdoers
settings.when: On the title's view, during David's exile from the sanctuary. On scholars' view, perhaps after the exile, when some Israelites were drawn to share the life and feasts of the powerful.
settings.why: To offer prayer as an evening sacrifice, and to ask God to keep the singer's own mouth and heart from evil before asking to be kept from the evil of others.
settings.readers: For those far from the temple, in exile or in the Diaspora, it taught that a prayer could rise like incense wherever they were.

title: A Prayer in the Cave
sum: Psalm 142 (Greek and Latin Psalm 141) is headed as David's prayer "when he was in the cave". He pours out his worry before God; when his spirit sinks, God knows his path, though a snare has been hidden on it. He looks to his right side, where a defender should stand, and no one is there.
So he cries to the LORD as his place of shelter and his share in the land of the living, and asks to be led out of the prison, so that the righteous will gather around him.

views.H: The title places it in a cave where David hid from Saul, Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1) or En-gedi (1 Samuel 24:3). Psalm 57 has the same setting. Rashi chooses En-gedi, where David cut the hem of Saul's robe.
views.C: Scholars read it as an individual lament, with the title added by editors who linked it to David's life. The "prison" (142:7) may be a real prison, or a picture of distress. It is one of thirteen psalms with a title naming an event in David's life.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 141. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Evening Prayer I of Sunday in week I, after Psalm 141. Thomas of Celano reports that Francis of Assisi died in 1226 praying it ("I cried to the Lord with my voice").
views.J: Rashi reads it in the cave at En-gedi. "My allotted share in the land of the living" (142:5) recalls the Levites, whose share was the LORD himself (Numbers 18:20).
views.X: Some Christian readers, from Augustine on, heard it as the prayer of Christ, deserted by his friends before his death (compare Mark 14:50). Francis of Assisi's death with this psalm on his lips made it beloved among Franciscans.

echoes: 1 Samuel 22:1; 1 Samuel 24:3; Psalm 57:0; Psalm 16:5; Numbers 18:20; Lamentations 3:24; Mark 14:50

settings.by: David, according to the title, hiding in a cave; one person with no defender
settings.to: God ("LORD", "you"), at first spoken of ("to him"), then addressed
settings.when: On the title's view, in the cave of Adullam or En-gedi, during Saul's pursuit. On scholars' view, a lament of anyone abandoned or imprisoned, later linked to David.
settings.why: To pour out distress before God when every human help has failed, and to claim God as one's only share.
settings.readers: For Israelites without land or influence after the exile, "my share in the land of the living" was a confession that God himself was their inheritance.

title: No One Alive Is in the Right
sum: Psalm 143 (Greek and Latin Psalm 142) is the last of the seven Penitential Psalms. The singer asks God to answer by his faithfulness and righteousness, but not to bring him to trial, since no living person is in the right before God. The enemy has crushed him and set him in darkness like the dead.

He remembers God's deeds of old and stretches out his hands like dry land. Then he asks for loyal love in the morning, for the road to walk on, and for God's good spirit to lead him on level ground. He ends, as a servant, asking God to silence his enemies.

views.H: Traditional readers place it in David's flight from Absalom. The Greek title in Codex Vaticanus and the Gallican Latin adds "when his son pursues him".
views.C: Scholars read it as an individual lament, built from many lines found in other psalms and in Lamentations (143:3 has the words of Lamentations 3:6, two of them reversed). Many date it after the exile. Its stress on God's righteousness as rescue is close to Isaiah 40–55, the chapters many scholars call Second Isaiah.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 142. It is the seventh Penitential Psalm (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), prayed in Lent and on Ash Wednesday in many churches. In the Byzantine rite it is one of the six psalms read at the start of Matins (Orthros).
views.J: Rashi reads 143:3 as the voice of Israel in Babylon. Jewish readers hear 143:2 as a confession that no one can stand before God on his own merit, the spirit of the daily prayers of supplication (tachanun), which ask for grace.
views.X: Paul echoes 143:2 in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16: no flesh will be put in the right before God by works of the law. Luther counted Psalm 143 among the "Pauline psalms" (with 32, 51 and 130), because it teaches that righteousness is God's gift. In 143:10 Codex Vaticanus has "your holy spirit" and the Targum "your holy spirit, the good one" (other Greek copies have "good"), and Christians read the verse of the Holy Spirit's guidance.

deep.b: "Do not go to trial with your servant, for no living person is in the right in your presence." Paul uses this line twice, adding "by works of the law" (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16), to show that no one is acquitted before God by keeping the law. Catholics, Lutherans, the Reformed and others agree that the psalm teaches the need of grace; they differ on how that grace makes one right, a question treated on the justification topic. In the psalm itself, the remedy is God's righteousness, not the singer's: "Answer me by your faithfulness, by your righteousness" (143:1). Jewish readers also hear the verse as a confession that no one can stand before God except by his mercy.

echoes: Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16; Lamentations 3:6; Psalm 130:3; Nehemiah 9:20; Isaiah 63:10–14; Job 9:2

settings.what: An individual lament and plea for guidance; a Penitential Psalm
settings.by: David, according to the title; one person pursued by an enemy, who calls himself God's servant
settings.when: On the title's view, and that of the Greek title in Codex Vaticanus, during Absalom's revolt. On scholars' view, after the exile, from its use of Lamentations and earlier psalms.
settings.why: To ask for rescue without claiming to be in the right, appealing only to God's faithfulness, righteousness and loyal love.
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, which knew it had been judged for its sins, the psalm taught it to ask for rescue by grace and for God's spirit to lead it on level ground.

title: The King's New Song
sum: Psalm 144 (Greek and Latin Psalm 143) begins as a king's praise, reusing lines from David's victory song, Psalm 18: the LORD is his rock, who trains his hands for war, his loyal love, fortress and shield. Then, like Psalm 8, it asks what a human being is, and answers: a puff of air.

The king asks God to come down in storm and lightning, to rescue him from "sons of foreign lands" who lie, and promises a new song on the ten-string harp. The last verses picture a people at peace, with tall sons, fine daughters, full barns and no cry in the streets, and end: Happy is the people whose God is the LORD.

views.H: Traditional readers take it as David's song after victory. Most Greek copies add "Against Goliath" to the title (Codex Alexandrinus does not), linking 144:10 ("the deadly sword") with the battle of 1 Samuel 17.
views.C: Most scholars read it as a late composition that gathers phrases from Psalms 18, 8, 33 and 104 into a royal prayer, perhaps for the hoped-for king after the exile. Many think 144:12–15 was a separate blessing joined to it.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 143. 144:15 is said in the synagogue just before Psalm 145, in Ashrei. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Evening Prayer.
views.J: Rashi applies the psalm to David's wars, and notes that the Masoretes count 144:2 among the places that read "my people" but mean "peoples". Its last verse, with 84:4, introduces Ashrei three times each day.
views.X: Christian readers have heard the king of 144:10 as Christ, "the one who hands kings their rescue", and the new song of 144:9 as the song of the redeemed (Revelation 5:9). Augustine read the peace of 144:12–15 as the true happiness of those whose God is the Lord, set against the wealth of the foreigners in the Greek reading.

deep.b: Psalm 144:1–11 reuses Psalm 18 freely. "Blessed is the LORD, my rock, who teaches my hands to fight a war" (144:1) draws on Psalm 18:34 and 18:46; "my fortress, my high tower, the one who gets me free, my shield, the one I take shelter in" (144:2) on Psalm 18:2; "bend your sky low and come down" (144:5) on 18:9; "flash your lightning and scatter them; shoot your arrows" (144:6) on 18:14; "pull me out of the great waters" (144:7) on 18:16; and "sons of foreign lands" (144:7, 11) on 18:44. But the mood is different. Psalm 18 looks back on victory; Psalm 144 asks for it, and between the borrowings it puts the question of Psalm 8, "what is a human being?", with the answer of 39:5, "a puff of air". The king is not a hero but a mortal who depends on God.

echoes: Psalm 18:2; Psalm 18:34; Psalm 18:46; Psalm 8:4; Psalm 39:5; Psalm 33:2–3; Psalm 33:12; 1 Samuel 17:45–51; Revelation 5:9

settings.by: David, according to the title; a king ("who frees David his servant")
settings.when: On the title's view, in David's wars; the Greek names the fight with Goliath. On many scholars' view, after the exile, a prayer for the coming king made from older psalms.
settings.why: To praise God as the king's strength while confessing the king's own frailty, and to ask for rescue from lying foreign enemies.
settings.readers: For those waiting after the exile, it kept alive the hope of a king from David's line whom God would rescue.
views: The title, the Greek title and traditional readers.
Most critical scholars, from its reuse of Psalm 18 and other psalms.

settings.when: Uncertain; perhaps once a separate harvest or temple blessing.
settings.why: To picture the peace and plenty that follow when God rescues the king and the people.
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, a picture of what Happy is the people whose God is the LORD would look like in daily life.

title: Every Day I Will Bless You
sum: Psalm 145 (Greek and Latin Psalm 144) is the last psalm headed "of David" and the only one called "a praise". It is an alphabet poem: its verses begin with the Hebrew letters in order, alef (145:1), bet (145:2), gimel (145:3), dalet (145:4), he (145:5), waw (145:6), zayin (145:7), chet (145:8), tet (145:9), yod (145:10), kaf (145:11), lamed (145:12), mem (145:13a–b), nun (145:13c, missing in the Masoretic Text), samekh (145:14), ayin (145:15), pe (145:16), tsade (145:17), qof (145:18), resh (145:19), shin (145:20) and tav (145:21).

The singer vows to bless God every day, and the praise spreads from one voice to every generation and to all flesh. At its center stand God's character, gracious and compassionate, good to all, and his kingdom, which lasts through every age. God holds up the falling, feeds every creature from his open hand, and is near to all who call on him truly.

views.H: Traditional readers take the title at face value: David's praise of God as King, the crown of his psalms. The Talmud treats it as David's.
views.C: Most scholars date it after the exile and read it as a learned alphabet hymn that gathers the creed of Exodus 34:6 and the praise of God's kingdom. Its place at the end of Book V's last David collection makes David bow before God the King, just before the final Hallel (146–150).
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 144. In Christian worship 145:15–16 has long been a grace before meals, in monasteries and in Luther's Small Catechism. The Roman Liturgy of the Hours sings it at Evening Prayer, and the Revised Common Lectionary appoints it often, including for the feeding of the five thousand.
views.J: With 84:4 and 144:15 before it and 115:18 after it, Psalm 145 is Ashrei, said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon. The Talmud promises the world to come to whoever says it three times a day, because it is an alphabet poem and because it contains "You open your hand" (Berakhot 4b), and it explains the missing nun line by Amos 5:2. In the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran each verse is followed by a refrain, "Blessed be the LORD and blessed be his name for ever and ever".
views.X: Christians read the kingdom lines (145:11–13) with Jesus' preaching of the kingdom, and 145:8–9 as the Old Testament's summary of God's character, fulfilled in Christ. The Greek's nun line, "the Lord is faithful in his words", was sung in the Greek and Latin churches.

deep.b: Every letter of the alphabet has a verse in Psalm 145 except nun, between mem (145:13) and samekh (145:14) in the Masoretic Text. The rabbis took the gap as deliberate: the verse beginning with nun that David avoided would have recalled Amos 5:2, "Fallen is the virgin Israel", and the next verse lifts the fallen (Berakhot 4b). But the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a), copied about a thousand years before the Leningrad Codex, has the line: "God is faithful in his words and loyal in all his works." The Greek has it with "the Lord" and "holy", and so does Jerome's Gallican Psalter. BHS reports it in the Syriac and in one medieval Hebrew manuscript, Kennicott 142, where it is added at the foot of the page. A fourteenth-century psalter in Cambridge (MS Or. 929) has it in its Hebrew column, but that column was copied beside Greek and Syriac columns that have the line, so it is not an independent witness. Against the line stand the Leningrad Codex, the other Hebrew manuscripts, the Targum and Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew. The weightiest objection is that the Qumran scroll is expansionist in this very psalm: it adds a refrain after every verse, retitles it "A prayer" and changes "who love him" to "who fear him" (145:20). The line's second half also repeats 145:17b, and the witnesses word it differently. The Plain prints it, as most modern versions do, because an alphabet poem implies it and two ancient witnesses have it; the variant gives the readings, and readers who follow the Masoretic Text can leave it out.

Ashrei ("Happy") is the Jewish name for Psalm 145 as said in the synagogue, after its first word in the two verses placed before it (84:4; 144:15). Psalm 115:18 is added at the end, so that the prayer ends in "Praise the LORD!". It is said twice in the morning, once in the opening psalms (Pesukei de-Zimra) and once near the end of the service, and once at the start of the afternoon service, three times each day as the Talmud recommends. At 145:16 worshipers pay special attention, and many touch their tefillin. The psalm thus links the morning praise with the daily psalms 146–150 that follow it in the prayer book.

echoes: Exodus 34:6–7; Daniel 4:3; Daniel 4:34; Amos 5:2; Deuteronomy 4:7; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Matthew 6:26; Luke 1:33

settings.what: An alphabet hymn of praise to God the King
settings.by: David, according to the title; one voice ("I") that calls on all flesh
settings.to: God ("my God, the King", "you"), and in some verses the listening congregation ("his")
settings.when: On the title's view, from David. On most scholars' view, after the exile, from a circle that composed alphabet poems for teaching and worship.
settings.why: To praise God fully, from first letter to last, for his greatness, goodness and kingdom, and to teach that praise to every generation.
settings.readers: For Israel under foreign kings, it confessed that God's kingdom lasts through every generation; in the synagogue it became the daily prayer of everyone.

title: Do Not Trust in Princes
sum: Psalm 146 (Greek and Latin Psalm 145) opens the final five psalms, each of which begins and ends with "Praise the LORD!" (hallelu-yah). The singer vows to praise God as long as he lives, and warns against trusting nobles: they die, return to the ground, and their plans die with them.

Happy is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, maker of heaven, earth and sea, who keeps faith forever. Then a list of what the LORD does: justice for the oppressed, bread for the hungry, freedom for prisoners, sight for the blind, care for foreigners, orphans and widows. The LORD will be king forever.

views.H: The Greek title names Haggai and Zechariah, the prophets of the rebuilt temple, as authors or singers of Psalms 146–148. Traditional readers have taken this as a sign that these psalms were sung at the second temple.
views.C: Most scholars date the psalm after the exile and read Psalms 146–150 as the Psalter's closing doxology, a closing burst of praise, composed or arranged by its editors. Its list of God's deeds draws on Deuteronomy and on Isaiah 61.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 145. In the synagogue it is the first of the five daily psalms (146–150) of the morning service. The Revised Common Lectionary appoints it in Advent and in Ordinary Time.
views.J: Jewish morning blessings echo 146:7–8 ("who frees the captives", "who opens the eyes of the blind"). Its last verse closes the Kedushah. The Talmud's wish to be among those who complete the Hallel every day is understood of Psalms 145–150 (Shabbat 118b, with Rashi).
views.X: Christians hear 146:7–8 in Jesus' words at Nazareth (Luke 4:18) and in his answer to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:5): what the LORD does in the psalm, Jesus does. The apostles' prayer in Acts 4:24 takes up 146:6.

deep.b: Each of the last five psalms begins and ends with hallelu-yah, "Praise the LORD!", so that the Psalter closes with ten of them. The praise widens step by step: one soul (146:1), Jerusalem (147:12), all creation in heaven and on earth (148), the assembly of the loyal (149), and finally everything that breathes (150:6). In Jewish tradition these are the daily psalms of the morning service, together with 145. In the Greek the hallelujahs move into the headings, and three of the psalms are credited to Haggai and Zechariah. Psalm 147 is divided in the Greek, so that the numbering, one behind since Psalm 10, comes back into line at Psalm 148.

echoes: Exodus 15:18; Exodus 20:11; Genesis 3:19; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18; Matthew 11:5; Acts 4:24; Psalm 118:8–9

settings.what: A hymn of praise, opening the final Hallel
settings.by: An unnamed singer ("my soul"), who also teaches ("Do not rely on nobles")
settings.to: His own soul, then the congregation, and at the end Zion
settings.when: After the exile, in most scholars' view; the Greek title names Haggai and Zechariah, prophets of the late 500s BC.
settings.why: To praise God for as long as one lives, and to teach that he alone, not human rulers, can be trusted to save.
settings.readers: For Israel under Persian and later rulers, it said that no prince would save them, and that the God of Jacob cares for the weakest.

title: He Counts the Stars
sum: Psalm 147 is one psalm in Hebrew but two in the Greek and Latin: Greek and Latin Psalm 146 is 147:1–11, and Greek and Latin Psalm 147 is 147:12–20. The first half praises the God who rebuilds Jerusalem, gathers its outcasts, heals the broken-hearted and counts and names the stars; who brings rain, grass and food for animals and ravens, and who enjoys not the strength of horses but those who fear him.

The second half calls Jerusalem to praise: God has strengthened its gates, blessed its children, given peace and the best of the wheat. His word runs to the earth, bringing snow, frost and ice, and then the thaw. And he has given his words, his rules and rulings, to Israel as to no other nation.
readings: The Hebrew tradition keeps it together: three calls to praise (147:1, 7, 12), each followed by reasons drawn from Jerusalem, creation and the word.
The Greek and Latin tradition divides it; the second part, Lauda Jerusalem, became a separate hymn of the church.

views.H: The Greek titles of both halves name Haggai and Zechariah, linking the psalm with the rebuilding of the temple after the exile. Traditional readers have connected 147:2 with Nehemiah's walls.
views.C: Scholars agree that it comes from after the exile, from its late words and its echoes of Isaiah 40–66, Job and Deuteronomy. Some think the two halves were once separate psalms; others see three stanzas of one hymn.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalms 146 and 147. In the synagogue it is one of the five daily psalms. In Latin Vespers the second half, Lauda Jerusalem, was sung on feasts of Mary, set by Monteverdi (1610) and Vivaldi; in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours both halves are used at Morning Prayer.
views.J: Rashi explains the young ravens (147:9) from the teaching that the raven neglects its young and God feeds them, and the cold of 147:17 as measured to what each person can bear. The verse "He tells his words to Jacob" (147:19) is read of the gift of the Torah to Israel.
views.X: Jesus' words about the ravens (Luke 12:24) and about God's care echo 147:9. Paul's "to them were entrusted the oracles of God" (Romans 3:2) restates 147:19–20. Christian readers have heard the word that runs swiftly (147:15) with John 1, the Word through whom all things were made.

echoes: Isaiah 40:26–28; Isaiah 56:8; Isaiah 61:1; Isaiah 55:10–11; Job 38:41; Luke 12:24; Deuteronomy 4:7–8; Romans 3:2; Psalm 33:16–18; Psalm 104:14

settings.what: A hymn of praise (Greek and Latin Psalm 146)
settings.by: An unnamed singer speaking for the congregation ("our God")
settings.when: After the exile, as Jerusalem was rebuilt and its exiles gathered; the Greek names Haggai and Zechariah.
settings.why: To praise the God whose greatness counts the stars and whose care heals the broken and feeds the ravens.
settings.readers: For the returning exiles, it joined the rebuilding of the city to the God who made and sustains the world.

settings.what: A hymn calling Jerusalem to praise (Greek and Latin Psalm 147)
settings.by: The same singer, or a temple choir
settings.when: After the walls and gates were rebuilt, perhaps in Nehemiah's time.
settings.why: To praise God for peace and plenty, for his word in the weather, and above all for his law given to Israel.
settings.readers: For the restored community, it taught that their peace was God's gift and that their law was a privilege no other nation had.

title: Praise from the Heavens and the Earth
sum: Psalm 148 (Greek and Latin Psalm 148) calls the whole creation to praise the LORD. First the heavens: angels, armies, sun, moon and stars, the highest heavens and the waters above them, all made at his command and set in place by a rule that will not be broken.

Then the earth: sea monsters and ocean depths, fire, hail, snow and storm, mountains, trees, animals and birds, kings and peoples, young men and women, old and young. Let them all praise his name, which alone stands high. He has raised a horn for his people Israel, a people near to him.

views.H: The Greek title names Haggai and Zechariah, as for Psalms 146–147. Traditional readers have read it as a temple hymn of the second temple.
views.C: Scholars read it as a hymn after the exile, with a list of creatures like the ancient "lists" of wisdom (compare Job 38–39) and an order like Genesis 1. The last verse (148:14) ties the praise of all creation to God's care for Israel.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 148, where the two systems agree again. With 149 and 150 it closed Morning Prayer every day in the Roman and Benedictine rites; Lauds takes its name from their Laudate. In the Byzantine rite these are the "Praises" (Ainoi) of Matins. It inspired Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Creatures and hymns such as "Praise the Lord! Ye Heavens Adore Him".
views.J: It is one of the five daily psalms of the morning service. The later Jewish work Pereq Shirah gives each creature its own verse of praise, in the spirit of this psalm. Rashi reads the rule of 148:6 as the decree that the sun serves by day and the moon by night.
views.X: The Song of the Three Young Men, added to Daniel 3 in the Greek, calls on the creatures very much in the order of this psalm, and is sung as the Benedicite in many churches. Christian readers take 148:14, the horn raised for God's people, with Luke 1:69, and see creation's praise as fulfilled in Revelation 5:13.

deep.h: Psalm 148 and the Song of the Three
deep.b: The Greek book of Daniel adds a long song sung by the three young men in the furnace (Daniel 3:52–90 in Catholic Bibles; the Song of the Three in the Protestant Apocrypha). It calls on angels, heavens, waters, sun and moon, stars, rain and dew, winds, fire and heat, cold, ice and snow, nights and days, light and darkness, mountains, plants, springs, seas, sea creatures, birds, animals and humans to bless the Lord, very much in the order of Psalm 148. Whether the song draws on the psalm or both draw on a common pattern, the church has sung the two together at Lauds. Psalm 148 also stands behind Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Creatures (1225), with its "Brother Sun" and "Sister Moon".

echoes: Genesis 1:1–31; Job 38:4–38; Psalm 103:20–22; Psalm 104:1–35; Jeremiah 31:35–36; Luke 1:69; Revelation 5:13

settings.what: A hymn calling all creation to praise
settings.by: An unnamed singer, or the temple choir
settings.to: Creation: first the heavens and their hosts, then the earth and its creatures, then human beings
settings.when: After the exile, in most scholars' view; the Greek title names Haggai and Zechariah.
settings.why: To call every created thing to praise its maker, and to place Israel's praise within the praise of the whole world.
settings.readers: For a small people in a large empire, it taught that the God of Israel is praised by sun, sea and kings, and that he has lifted up their horn.

title: A New Song and a Sword
sum: Psalm 149 (Greek and Latin Psalm 149) calls the assembly of God's loyal ones to sing a new song: Israel is to rejoice in its maker and Zion's children in their King, with dance, tambourine and lyre, for the LORD is pleased with his people and crowns the lowly with victory.

Then the tone changes. With God's praise in their throats and a double-edged sword in their hands, the loyal are to bring vengeance on the nations, bind their kings in chains, and carry out the sentence that is written. This, the psalm says, is the glory of all his loyal ones.
readings: Some read it as a song for Israel's army, as in 2 Chronicles 20:21–22, or as a hope for victory over oppressors after the exile, perhaps in the Maccabean wars.
Others read the sword as the final judgment of the nations, written in advance (149:9), in which God's people share (Daniel 7:22).
Rashi reads the praises themselves as the sword; Christians link the two-edged sword to the word of God (Hebrews 4:12).

views.H: Traditional readers have read it of David's victories, or of the battles of Israel's history, and Rashi of the end of days, with the judgment "written" in Ezekiel 25:14.
views.C: Scholars date it after the exile. Some place it in the Maccabean age (160s BC), when the "Hasideans" (chasidim) fought for the law; most think it older, a hymn about the end of the age and the judgment of the nations.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 149. With 148 and 150 it closed Morning Prayer daily in the Western church and is part of the "Praises" of Byzantine Matins. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Sunday Morning Prayer in week I.
views.J: It is one of the five daily morning psalms. Rashi reads the sword as the praises in their mouths and the written judgment as Ezekiel's prophecy against Edom. The Midrash on Psalms stresses that vengeance belongs to God and falls on the kings who attacked Israel.
views.X: Christian readers have usually read the sword spiritually, as the word of God (Hebrews 4:12; Ephesians 6:17; Revelation 1:16), and the judgment as Christ's at the end (1 Corinthians 6:2). Delitzsch warned that a literal reading was used to stir up religious wars, by Caspar Schoppe in the Thirty Years' War and by Thomas Müntzer in the Peasants' War.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 20:21–22; Nehemiah 4:17–18; Ezekiel 25:14; Daniel 7:22; Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 1:16; Revelation 19:15; 1 Corinthians 6:2; Psalm 96:1

settings.by: An unnamed singer calling the assembly ("the gathering of his loyal ones")
settings.to: The assembly of Israel, called to praise
settings.when: After the exile; some scholars think of the Maccabean wars of the 160s BC, most of a hope for the end-time judgment of the nations.
settings.why: To celebrate God as Israel's maker and king, and to look forward to the defeat of the powers that oppressed his people.
settings.readers: For Israel under foreign kings, it promised that the oppressors' kings would one day be bound, and that the lowly would be crowned with victory.
views: Some scholars, from the sword and the "loyal ones".
Most scholars, from the "written" sentence and the judgment of the nations.

title: Let Everything That Breathes Praise
sum: Psalm 150 (Greek and Latin Psalm 150) closes the Book of Psalms. It has no petition and no reason except God himself: praise him in his holy place and in the dome of his power, for his mighty deeds and his vast greatness. Then every instrument is called in: ram's horn, harp and lyre, tambourine and dance, strings and pipe, cymbals soft and loud.

The last line reaches beyond all instruments to every breathing thing. The psalm is the doxology (closing blessing of praise) of Book V and of the whole Psalter, which began with one happy person meditating on God's law (1:1–2) and ends with all that breathes praising Yah. In the Greek, Psalm 151 follows it, marked "outside the number".

views.H: Traditional readers take it as the closing hymn of David's collected psalms, sung with the instruments David appointed for the Levites (1 Chronicles 15:16; 23:5).
views.C: Scholars read it as a hymn composed or placed by the editors of the Psalter as its final doxology, matching the blessings that close Books I–IV (41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48). It lists the instruments of the second temple, priestly, Levitical and popular together.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 150; the Greek then adds Psalm 151. It closed Morning Prayer every day in the Western church with 148 and 149, and it is part of the "Praises" of Byzantine Matins. Composers from Bruckner and Franck to Stravinsky (Symphony of Psalms) and Britten have set it. In the synagogue it ends the five daily psalms.
views.J: It is the last of the daily morning psalms, and its last verse is repeated in the prayer book to mark the end of the Psalter. The Talmud's "those who complete the Hallel every day" is understood of 145–150 (Shabbat 118b, with Rashi).
views.X: Christian readers have heard it as the song of the whole creation fulfilled in Revelation 5:13. Augustine read the instruments as figures of the saints and their virtues, and the debate over whether its instruments belong in church worship is described below.

deep.h: The doxology of the whole Psalter
deep.b: Each of the first four books of the Psalms ends with a blessing: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel" (41:13; compare 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48). Book V has none of its own; instead Psalm 150, perhaps with all of 146–150, takes that place for Book V and for the whole Psalter. The shape of the book moves from lament to praise. Its first psalm speaks of the happy person who delights in God's law (1:1–2); its last of everything that breathes praising Yah (150:6). Many scholars, following Claus Westermann and Walter Brueggemann, see in this movement the book's message: lament is real, but praise has the last word.

In the Greek Psalter, Psalm 150 is followed by Psalm 151, headed "This psalm is written by David himself, and is outside the number, when he fought Goliath alone". It is Scripture for the Orthodox churches, and in an appendix for some others; it is not in the Hebrew Bible or the site's Plain, and the book page and works page treat it. The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) has a longer Hebrew form of it in two parts (151A and 151B), but not after Psalm 150: there Psalm 150 is followed by a hymn to the Creator, and the Psalm 151 texts stand at the very end of the scroll, after Psalms 140 and 134. A Psalms scroll from Masada (MasPs-b) appears to end with Psalm 150, as Shemaryahu Talmon reported, which agrees with the order of the Masoretic Psalter.

echoes: Psalm 1:1–2; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 106:48; 1 Chronicles 15:16; 1 Chronicles 16:5; Genesis 1:6–8; Genesis 2:7; Revelation 5:13

settings.what: The closing hymn and doxology of the Psalter
settings.by: An unnamed singer, or the temple choir
settings.to: Everyone and everything: the worshipers, the musicians, and finally every breathing thing
settings.when: After the exile, in most scholars' view, when the Psalter was given its final shape; the instruments are those of the second temple.
settings.why: To end the book of prayers in pure praise, with every instrument and every living creature.
settings.readers: For those who prayed the whole Psalter after the exile, it said that their laments, curses and thanks all led to the praise of God.

traditions.q: Psalm 150 calls for horn, harp, drum and cymbals. Is it a pattern for church worship, or a picture of praise?
views: The fathers, such as Augustine, read the instruments as figures of the saints and their virtues; the Second Vatican Council holds the pipe organ "in high esteem" and allows other instruments that suit sacred use (Sacrosanctum Concilium 120), so the psalm is both a picture and a warrant.

Byzantine and Slavic services are sung without instruments. The psalm is sung every morning at Matins, but its instruments are read as the members of the body and the powers of the soul tuned to praise, following the fathers.
Lutherans have taken the psalm as a warrant for the organ and for instruments in church, which they count as free gifts, neither commanded nor forbidden.

Calvin held that instruments belonged to the time of the law, like the temple's sacrifices. Reformed Presbyterians who sing only psalms sing Psalm 150 unaccompanied; most Reformed churches today use instruments.

Churches of Christ sing Psalm 150 without instruments: it belongs to the old covenant, and the New Testament names only singing for the church. Christian Churches in the same movement use instruments.
Pentecostal and charismatic churches take Psalm 150 literally, as a call to praise with every instrument, with loud cymbals and with dancing.
